marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q001.takeaway: Lateral pterygoid depresses and protrudes mandible and assists side-to-side movement.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q001.displayText: The marked insertion is on the mandible for the lateral pterygoid muscle. The action of this muscle is depression, protrusion and side-to-side movement of the jaw. Lateral pterygoid originates from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of sphenoid and from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate. It inserts into the pterygoid fovea, capsule of the temporomandibular joint and articular disc.

rationales.b: Elevation and protrusion is associated with lateral pterygoid plus elevators, but its source action includes depression, not elevation.
rationales.c: Temporalis elevates/retracts the mandible; lateral pterygoid instead protrudes and depresses.
rationales.d: Lateral pterygoid depresses and protrudes; retraction is mainly posterior temporalis.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q002.takeaway: Temporalis elevates mandible; posterior fibers also retract.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q002.displayText: The marked muscle is the temporalis, whose main action is elevation of the mandible. Other actions are side-to-side grinding movements of the mandible, and the posterior fibers help retract the mandible.

rationales.b: Depression is chiefly produced by suprahyoid muscles and lateral pterygoid, not temporalis.
rationales.c: Protrusion is an action of lateral pterygoid, not the main action of temporalis.
rationales.d: Retraction is an additional action of posterior temporalis fibers, but elevation is the main action.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q003.takeaway: Lateral pterygoid muscle (label B) helps open the jaw.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q003.displayText: The structure marked B represents the lateral pterygoid muscle, which is responsible for opening the mouth. Lateral pterygoid originates from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of sphenoid and the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate; inserts into the pterygoid fovea, capsule of the temporomandibular joint and articular disc; and is supplied by the lateral pterygoid nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve. Other structures marked in the figure are A temporalis, C masseter, and D medial pterygoid.

rationales.a: Label A is not the muscle identified in the source diagram as opening the mouth.
rationales.c: Label C identifies another muscle; lateral pterygoid is the jaw-opening muscle shown at B.
rationales.d: Label D is not the source-marked lateral pterygoid muscle.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q004.takeaway: Excessive lateral pterygoid contraction can dislocate TMJ anteriorly during wide opening.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q004.displayText: Anterior temporomandibular-joint dislocation occurs due to excessive contraction of the lateral pterygoid, classically with extreme mouth opening such as yawning, laughing, vomiting or dental treatment. Some fibers of the upper head of the lateral pterygoid insert into the capsule of the TMJ and the anterior/medial borders of the articular disc. Contraction can pull the disc forward; excessive opening can cause anterior displacement of the joint. Superior and posterior dislocations are rare and associated with high-energy trauma.
emphasis: excessive contraction of the lateral pterygoid

rationales.a: Temporalis elevates and retracts mandible; it is not the primary muscle whose excessive contraction pulls the condyle anteriorly.
rationales.c: Buccinator compresses cheek and does not produce TMJ dislocation.
rationales.d: Masseter elevates mandible; the source links anterior dislocation during wide opening to lateral pterygoid.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q005.takeaway: Trigeminal motor fibers run with mandibular (V3), not maxillary (V2), division.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q005.displayText: The findings are suggestive of herpes zoster involving the trigeminal nerve. The false statement is that motor innervation is exclusively carried by the maxillary division. Motor fibers are carried by the mandibular division. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the largest cranial nerve and has ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions. V1 supplies sensation to the scalp, cornea, conjunctiva, iris, upper eyelid, lacrimal gland, forehead and mucous membranes of the nose. V2 supplies lower eyelid, cheeks, maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, lateral nose, upper lip, palate, teeth and gingiva. V3 supplies sensation to the chin/lower lip, temporal membrane, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric and mandibular teeth, and provides motor supply to the muscles of mastication, tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.

rationales.a: Trigeminal nerve is predominantly sensory overall, but the false statement is assigning motor fibers to V2.
rationales.c: Corneal sensation is primarily carried by ophthalmic division, a true statement.
rationales.d: Medial pterygoid receives motor fibers from mandibular division, a true statement.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q006.takeaway: Lateral pterygoid is supplied by its own V3 branch, not nerve to medial pterygoid.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q006.displayText: The site marked X is the mandibular foramen containing the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve. The muscles medial pterygoid, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini are supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid, which arises from the trunk of the mandibular nerve. Lateral pterygoid is supplied by a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve.

rationales.a: Medial pterygoid is supplied by nerve to medial pterygoid from V3.
rationales.b: Tensor tympani is supplied by nerve to medial pterygoid, a V3 motor branch.
rationales.c: Tensor veli palatini also receives nerve to medial pterygoid; lateral pterygoid receives a separate anterior-division branch.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q007.takeaway: Auriculotemporal nerve mediates Frey syndrome after parotid surgery.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q007.displayText: The presentation is Frey's syndrome, involving the auriculotemporal nerve, marked 2. The other numbered structures are maxillary nerve, posterior auricular nerve and inferior alveolar nerve. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of mandibular nerve and provides cutaneous sensation to the tragus and adjoining external acoustic meatus and to the auricle/scalp. It carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid. After parotid surgery, aberrant regeneration of these fibers to sweat glands and skin vessels causes gustatory sweating, warmth and redness during salivation.

rationales.a: Label 3 is not auriculotemporal nerve in the source image.
rationales.b: Label 1 is not the auriculotemporal nerve; it identifies another infratemporal structure.
rationales.c: Label 4 is not the nerve associated with Frey syndrome; source marks auriculotemporal nerve 2.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q008.takeaway: TMJ rotation occurs in inferior joint compartment below disc.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q008.displayText: Rotatory movements of the jaw take place in the joint space below the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint. The temporomandibular joint is adapted to both gliding and rotary movement. The capsular ligament around the upper compartment is relatively loose and allows gliding/translation, while the lower compartment is tighter and allows rotational movement.

rationales.a: Upper compartment permits gliding/translation, while rotation occurs below disc.
rationales.c: The TMJ has upper and lower joint spaces separated by disc, not a separate medial compartment for rotation.
rationales.d: Intermediate zone is part of the disc, not the synovial space where hinge rotation occurs.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q009.takeaway: Superior oblique is supplied by CN IV.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q009.displayText: The marked muscle is the superior oblique muscle. It is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV). Superior oblique helps in looking downward and inward. There are seven extraocular muscles: levator palpebrae superioris, four recti, and two obliques. Lateral rectus is supplied by abducens (VI), superior oblique by trochlear (IV), and the remaining extraocular muscles by oculomotor (III).

rationales.a: Oculomotor nerve supplies most extraocular muscles but not superior oblique.
rationales.c: Trigeminal nerve supplies facial sensation and mastication, not superior oblique.
rationales.d: Abducens supplies lateral rectus; trochlear supplies superior oblique.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q010.takeaway: Medial rectus is supplied by inferior division of oculomotor nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q010.displayText: The medial rectus is paralyzed on the right side, leading to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and a divergent/lateral squint. Medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique are supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Oculomotor nerve has superior and inferior divisions in the orbit; superior division supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris, while inferior division supplies inferior rectus, medial rectus and inferior oblique.
emphasis: inferior division of the oculomotor nerve

rationales.a: Superior division supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae, not medial rectus.
rationales.b: Abducens supplies lateral rectus, whose unopposed action causes divergent squint.
rationales.d: Trochlear supplies superior oblique; medial rectus is supplied by inferior CN III division.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q011.takeaway: Superior oblique is not supplied by marked oculomotor nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q011.displayText: The marked structure is the oculomotor nerve. It does not supply superior oblique, which is supplied by the trochlear nerve. Among extraocular muscles, lateral rectus is supplied by abducens and superior oblique by trochlear; the rest are supplied by oculomotor.

rationales.a: Superior rectus is supplied by superior division of CN III, which is the marked nerve.
rationales.c: Medial rectus receives inferior-division CN III, so it is supplied by the marked nerve.
rationales.d: Levator palpebrae superioris receives superior division of CN III; superior oblique is supplied by trochlear.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q012.takeaway: Stapedius is supplied by facial nerve (CN VII).
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q012.displayText: Stapedius is supplied by the nerve to stapedius, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Injury causes stapedius paralysis and hyperacusis because stapedius and tensor tympani normally contract in response to loud noises to dampen vibration of the tympanic membrane and reduce oscillation of the ossicles. Paralysis increases sensitivity to sounds.

rationales.b: Vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing/balance, not motor fibers to stapedius.
rationales.c: Trigeminal nerve supplies mastication and facial sensation, not stapedius.
rationales.d: Abducens supplies lateral rectus, not stapedius.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q013.takeaway: Great auricular nerve is the large ascending cervical plexus branch.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q013.displayText: The thickened nerve marked by the arrow is the great auricular nerve. The other visible nerve is the transverse cervical nerve. The great auricular nerve is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds around the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends, dividing near the parotid into anterior and posterior branches. It supplies skin over the mastoid region, posteroinferior auricle, parotid region and angle of mandible. Clinical points include sensory loss after injury, Frey's syndrome relationship, and use in nerve grafting.
emphasis: second and third cervical spinal nerves

rationales.b: Lesser occipital nerve supplies scalp behind ear but is a smaller branch than the great auricular nerve.
rationales.c: Facial nerve provides motor supply to facial expression, not the thickened ascending sensory cervical plexus branch.
rationales.d: Auriculotemporal supplies temporal scalp/auricle and parotid secretomotor route, not the marked cervical nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q014.takeaway: Sternohyoid is a non-hybrid infrahyoid muscle supplied by ansa cervicalis.
marrow__ANAT_CH30_Q014.displayText: The sternohyoid muscle marked as 3 is not a hybrid muscle. It is innervated only by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C1-C3 via ansa cervicalis. Examples of hybrid muscles in the figure include trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, which receive motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve with proprioceptive fibers from cervical spinal nerves, and digastric, whose anterior and posterior bellies have different nerve supplies.

rationales.a: Muscle 1 is not the source-labeled sternohyoid.
rationales.b: Muscle 2 corresponds to another neck muscle; the source labels sternohyoid as 3.
rationales.d: Muscle 4 is not the sternohyoid; the source identifies number 3 as the non-hybrid muscle.
